audit.recode_to: Keep kind = fixed penult (penultimate prominence is what Jacottet 1906, Tucker 1929, Doke & Mofokeng 1957 §60 [via Kunene], Nussbaum & Lijane 1968 and Mixdorff et al. 2011 all describe), but (a) recode domain UNSTATED -> phrase/utterance: Tucker §250, Kunene §3.4 and Nussbaum & Lijane cycle 4 all state the penult lengthening sits on the penult of the statement/pause group (and of words in isolation), is absent on word-penults mid-sentence and is suppressed in questions; (b) add a caution: Kunene 1961 (UCT PhD, pp.153-167) holds that 'S.Sotho is not a stress language', that penult prominence is LENGTH, and that inherent word stress is on the root (stem-initial) syllable with only secondary stress on the penult in stems of 4+ syllables — an explicit challenge to Doke's penult-stress statement; (c) note that Jacottet's 'last syllable when it ends in ng' clause is penult-regular once final ŋ is counted as a syllabic nasal (cf. Kunene sefate:ng, Nussbaum ha-n-tle); (d) when a copy of Doke & Mofokeng 1957 is obtained, make §60 the deciding citation.
audit.reasoning: Quote check: Jacottet 1906:4 confirmed verbatim on the held page image; Tucker 1929:99-100 confirmed verbatim in the copy fetched sources now. The classification rests on a 1906 missionary teaching course plus a 1929 comparative-phonetics monograph whose examples are Tswana; Glottolog lists a 491-pp reference grammar (Doke & Mofokeng 1957, not open, not held) and a 497-pp phonology PhD (Kunene 1961, fetched sources now). Every source opened agrees the penult of a statement/isolation form is long/prominent, so the penult coding itself is not in danger, but (1) three opened sources say the phenomenon is utterance/phrase-level, so domain should not stay UNSTATED, and (2) Kunene 1961 explicitly disputes penult word stress (root-syllable inherent stress; penult = phrasal length), which the record does not mention. Hence 'thin' (old pedagogical deciding source, better sources exist, one of them dissenting on

sources.citation: Nussbaum, Loren V. & Lijane, Gershom T. 1968. An introduction to spoken Sesotho. Washington, DC: Center for Applied Linguistics (ERIC ED048592, 569 PDF pp.)
sources.quote: 'The penultimate (second to last) syllable of a statement is longer than other syllables. You can observe this lengthening on the /n/ in hantle and on the first /e/ in khotso ... This lengthening is automatic in statements, but ... it does not occur with questions. It also occurs when words or names are spoken in isolation: Thabo [aa], lebitso [ii].' Questions are marked 'by a raising of the entire pitch level ... and by an absence of penultimate lengthening'. (Syllabic nasal counts as the penult in ha.n.tle.)
sources.locator: Cycle 4, 'To the student' note (PDF p.26); also cycle 5 note (txt line 3487)
sources.note: Glottolog-listed course with an explicit domain statement (penult lengthening in statements and isolation words, absent in questions; syllabic nasal can be the lengthened penult) — supports recoding domain from UNSTATED.

sources.quote: Length §3.4: penult of a word/phrase/clause uttered non-interrogatively (or before pause+downstep) is long; short in questions; 'Length of the penult is thus the sole criterion for distinction between questions and statements' (examples incl. isolation words: Maso:pha, sefate:ng, waha:e). sources.note: Only full phonetic monograph on S. Sotho length and stress; separates phrase-penult LENGTH (statements/isolation, absent in questions) from inherent word STRESS, which it places on the root syllable, explicitly challenging Doke's penult stress — must be registered as a caution/dissent on this record.

sources.citation: Mixdorff, H., Mohasi, L., Machobane, M. & Niesler, T. 2011. A study on the perception of tone and intonation in Sesotho. Proc. Interspeech 2011, Florence. doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2011-796
sources.quote: Questions show 'a conspicuous shortening of the penultimate syllable which is the carrier of word stress in Sesotho'; perception test: shortening the penult to 70% is the strongest cue turning a statement into a question (instrumental, resynthesis-based).
sources.note: Modern instrumental support that the (utterance-)penult is the locus of prominence ('carrier of word stress') and that its lengthening is suspended in questions — upgrades evidence grade beyond 1906/1929 impressionistic sources.

sources.citation: Tucker, A. N. 1929. The comparative phonetics of the Suto-Chuana group of Bantu languages. London: Longmans, Green & Co. (archive.org item comparativephone0000tuck)
sources.quote: §250: 'In a normal statement, the penultimate syllable, whether a word in itself or part of a word, is pronounced long. ... This length is never found on the penultimate syllable of any word when it occurs in the middle of a sentence.' §251: in questions/commands the penult is not lengthened. §252: 'In a normal sentence, the last two syllables are both stressed ... the stress on the final syllable is subjective, while that on the penultimate syllable is primarily objective.' Examples 'from SeChuana'.
sources.note: Cited in the record as corroboration and as the domain quotation (dloc) but was not held; now on file so the §250-252 quotes are verifiable (confirmed).

sources.citation: Zerbian, Sabine & Barnard, Etienne. 2010. Word-level prosody in Sotho-Tswana. Proc. Speech Prosody 2010, Chicago. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2010-62
sources.quote: Tone-assignment model for Sotho-Tswana (data Northern Sotho); states that intonation-phrase boundaries 'determine the location of the penultimate lengthening and falling tone which are so salient in the Southern Bantu languages' and that yes/no questions lack penultimate lengthening. No word-stress claim specific to Southern Sotho.
